sentences.text: The animal is named Labrujasuchus expectatus.
Scientists know it from a partial associated skeleton containing forelimb material, vertebrae, hindlimb parts, and pubic region elements.
Its anatomy closely resembles that of the North American shuvosaurids Effigia and Shuvosaurus.
A large internal tuberosity, sometimes called a medial process, is present on the humerus, and the head of this bone is teardrop-shaped rather than D-shaped.
Unlike other North American shuvosaurids, Labrujasuchus has a hypertrophied ventral crest on the ischium, making the bone deeper than wide.
An anterior groove on the fibula, located just medial to the iliofibularis trochanter, is a distinguishing feature of the species.

The genus was described by Turner and colleagues, including Alan H. Turner, Ciara E. Kernan, Adam Laing, Adam C. Pritchard, Michelle R. Stocker, Randall B. Irmis, Nathan D. Smith, Sarah Werning, and Sterling J. Nesbitt.
This work established Labrujasuchus as a new genus and new species.
The holotype skeleton was discovered in 2006 at the Hayden Quarry at Ghost Ranch.
It comes from paleochannel H2, a specific layer dated to the mid Norian, approximately 211 million years ago.
Researchers referred additional fossils, including a left coracoid from channel H3 and a left tibia from channel H4, to the genus.
Labrujasuchus is classified as a member of the family Shuvosauridae within the superfamily Poposauroidea.
This creature lived during the Late Triassic period, specifically the Norian age, in the United States, with the type locality in the Chinle Formation of New Mexico.
A phylogenetic analysis by Turner et al. excluded the coeval shuvosaurid Sonselasuchus, which was named two months before Labrujasuchus.
